analysis.one_liner: Requires lenders to document who owns a mortgage and prove legal compliance before foreclosing on a home.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died in the House Financial Services Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred a lender or servicer from starting a foreclosure on a borrower's primary residence until it filed a detailed report identifying the actual holder of the mortgage note, the original lender, and every later assignee, and certifying compliance with federal lending and consumer-protection laws. It would also have required written notice to the homeowner at least five days before foreclosure proceedings began, including the amounts owed, deadlines to respond, and options like loan modification. It applied to both court-supervised and non-judicial foreclosures and set a national floor without overriding stronger state protections.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing foreclosure on the house they live in. They would learn, before losing their home, who actually holds the note, whether the loan was serviced lawfully, exactly what they owe, and what alternatives such as modification exist. Borrowers caught in the mass-assignment and robo-signing problems of the mortgage crisis would have a documented chain of ownership to challenge in court.

how_it_helps.text: Before any foreclosure could begin, the filer had to submit a report identifying the actual holder of the mortgage note, the originating lender, and all subsequent assignees, plus anyone else with an interest in the property [S3].

The report had to state whether the mortgage was made and serviced in compliance with major federal consumer laws, including the Truth in Lending Act, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, and whether any bona fide default had actually occurred [S3].

Homeowners had to receive written notice at least five days before foreclosure action, stating amounts in arrears, itemized fees, deadlines to raise defenses, and options such as workout, modification, and redemption [S3].
If violations were found, the report had to say whether the homeowner should get an extended right to rescind or redeem the mortgage beyond what state law allows [S3].
The bill covered both judicial and non-judicial foreclosures and applied only to mortgages on one- to four-family homes the borrower occupies as a principal residence [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and foreclosure law firms. Each foreclosure would require a report prepared by an independent party with no interest in the foreclosure, adding cost and time, and foreclosures with documentation gaps could be delayed or defeated. Some of that cost could be passed back to borrowers through fees.

drawbacks.text: The bill required a report by an independent party covering compliance with roughly ten federal statutes, plus borrower demographics, for every foreclosure on a primary residence. That is a heavy paperwork burden that would slow even legitimate foreclosures and could add fees to the very borrowers being foreclosed on [S3].

Extended rights to rescind or redeem a mortgage beyond state-law periods, triggered by any finding of noncompliance, would create lasting uncertainty about who owns foreclosed homes, which can depress sales of foreclosed properties and slow neighborhood recovery.
Delaying foreclosures is not costless: prolonged vacancies can harm surrounding property values and neighbors, a cost an honest supporter of foreclosure paperwork would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea answers a real grievance from the foreclosure crisis: lenders and servicers initiating foreclosures, sometimes without clean proof they held the note. Requiring documentation and plain-language notice before taking someone's home is a genuine protection. But the bill as written is blunt. It piles a sprawling, ten-statute compliance report on every case rather than targeting the documentation failures it was meant to catch, and the added delay and cost would fall partly on distressed borrowers and their neighborhoods. A narrower version would have been easier to defend.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill on January 4, 2013, the first day of the 113th Congress [S1].
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, and no further action was ever recorded on it [S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor at any point during the two-year Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and servicers came out ahead: they never faced the pre-foreclosure documentation and notice duties, and the foreclosure process continued as it was. Homeowners got no new protections.

for.name: Rep. Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 113th Congress and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat in committee for the entire two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. A single House Democrat sponsored the bill and no member of either party cosponsored it, so no partisan lineup formed around it.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to prove, through an independent report filed before any foreclosure, that they hold the note, identified every party with an interest, and complied with federal lending laws, plus five days of advance written notice to the borrower. Their interest in foreclosing quickly with minimal documentation ran directly against the bill's protections for homeowners, and with the bill's death they avoided all of these obligations.

industries.industry: Foreclosure law firms and document processing contractors
industries.note: A high-volume foreclosure practice built on streamlined, sometimes poorly documented filings would have faced new documentation requirements in every case. The bill's failure preserved the existing process.
